name: Kere
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Rarrick, Samantha Carol. 2017. A Tonal Grammar of Kere (Papuan) in Typological Perspective. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. ScholarSpace hdl 10125/62497 (open access).
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.2.1 'Stress', pp. 26-28; Sec. 2.2.2 'Rhythm' summary, p. 33; Sec. 3.3.7 'Tone and stress', pp. 112-114
catalog_quote: Kere has predictable stress, much like Hua (Haiman 1980). As mentioned above, stress in this language is indicated by vowel duration, and syllables with primary stress tend to be longer than others. ... At the word level, primary stress is initial, while secondary stress is assigned to alternating syllables from left to right, as seen in the examples of disyllabic, trisyllabic, and polysyllabic words below. Suffixation changes stress patterns only when it changes the number of syllables in a word. ... These words behave predictably based on their number of syllables, rather than on their number of morphemes, unlike Kuman (Hardie 2003). ... Looking at large phrases and narratives, it is clear that Kere relies on fixed word stress, like Czech, Polish, and Swahili (Ladefoged & Johnson 2011). Although at the phrasal level, there are some changes in stress to avoid the occurrence of two consecutive primary stresses, this language is quite consistent in its assignment of fixed word stress; primary stress is initial and alternating syllables receive secondary stress in following syllables, which are grouped into trochees.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Suffixation change…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and non-contrastive: primary stress on the first syllable of the (phonological) word, secondary stresses on every other syllable thereafter (left-to-right trochees), e.g. [ˈgil.suˌβɛ] 'pain', [ˈkɛb.naˌβa.i] 'younger sibling'. Stress is realised mainly as vowel duration; pitch is reserved for the independent lexical tone system (L/H), which does not directly interact with stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on alternating syllables after the initial, left to right (trochaic feet); a trisyllable gets secondary stress on its final syllable (degenerate foot), often repaired by medial vowel syncope; in compounds the non-head word takes secondary on its first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Proclitic subject pronoun + verb stressed as one word (primary on the pronoun); in compounds only one member keeps initial primary stress (choice predictable from foot count); phrase-initial monosyllables are demoted to secondary stress to avoid primary-primary clash; vowel syncope triggers re-footing.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly word-level rule (phonological word, including procliticised pronouns), with separate discussion of compound and phrasal stress/clash; measured from naturalistic narratives of two speakers (Praat durations). Kere is described as having contrastive lexical tone alongside this predictable stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Kere, a variety of Sinasina spoken in Du, Silma, Mondia and neighbouring villages (Glottolog dialect kere1300 under sina1271; ISO sst). Rarrick treats 'Sinasina' as a district label covering several tok ples varieties (Kere, Tabare, Gunangi, Dinga, Nimai, Kebai, Kondo) that differ mainly in lexical tone patterns; the older grammar (McVinney & Luzbetak) describes the Tabare variety (taba1262).

tone_statements.citation: Tebay, Sören E. 2025. Phrase-level Opacity as Shared Activity in Kere. Ms., Universität Leipzig, March 2025. 23 pp. LingBuzz lingbuzz/008937.
tone_statements.quote: Kere and Tabare exhibit lexical and tonal differences;; speakers say that the tonal differences are a true alternation (high in Kere where Tabare is low), but this claim needs to be confirmed. ... Also of interest is the tonal status of Kere. Tone and pitch are salient to speakers, and most are aware that one of the main differences between Kere and Tabare is “tune.” However, the tonal typology of Chimbu languages is not at all clear-cut.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.1 (pp. 26-28): Kere has predictable stress cued by vowel duration (not pitch); primary stress word-initial, secondary stress on alternating syllables left-to-right (trochaic feet); suffixation changes stress only by changing syllable count; compounds/phrases show clash avoidance (phrase-initial monosyllables demoted to secondary). Sec. 3.3.7 (pp. 112-114): stress and lexical tone do not directly interact; High tone barred from initial (stressed) syllables of polysyllables. Language has contrastive lexical tone (ch. 3, Table 5 p. 154/180).

tone.n_tones: 2 (H, L) per the Rarrick 2017 source it builds on
tone.says: Sec. 2 (pp. 2-4) restates Kere phrasal tonology from Rarrick 2017 ('SR') with H vs L tones on syllable/mora TBUs and three phrase-level processes: Upstep (a H after a H-toned TBU is upstepped, raising all following tones; SR 117-118), Low Deletion (a single L between two H-toned TBUs becomes H; SR 120-121) and Boundary Tone Shift (utterance-final L% inserted on the last TBU, shifting a final H to the penult; SR 148, 124); Boundary Tone Shift counterfeeds Low Deletion and Upstep, and Low Deletio…

tone.says: Sec. 2.4 'トーン' (pp. 163-168) argues tone correspondences are the key to East Simbu subgrouping. All Simbu languages are taken to be tone languages whose contrastive unit is a word-domain melody; five melody types H (high), F (falling), R (rising), L (low), D ('落調', key-lowering/downstep trigger = word-final floating L).
